note.text: A mixed economy combines market exchange with public action and different ownership arrangements. Private firms and households make many decisions, while public bodies may provide services, regulate activities or pursue distributional aims. The balance varies across countries and sectors. Mixed does not mean an exact equal split. Regulation is not the same thing as ownership: a private firm can be regulated without becoming publicly owned. Evaluate a particular policy through its purpose, mechanism, costs and effects.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: A mixed economy combines market exchange with public action and different ownership arrangements. Private firms and households make many decisions, while public bodies may provide services, regulate activities or pursue distributional aims. The balance varies across countries and sectors. Mixed does not mean an exact equal split. Regulation is not the same thing as ownership: a private firm can be regulated without becoming publicly owned. Evaluate a particular policy through its purpose, mechanism, costs and effects.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: A family stall can trade in a market while a public body maintains a road used by buyers and sellers. Rules about weights and product information can shape private exchange. The presence of both activities illustrates a mixed arrangement; it does not supply a numerical share for the whole economy or prove that every intervention works well.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: For each example, ask who owns the resource, who makes decisions and what public action is involved. Do not equate mixed with random or unplanned. Compare a policy's intended effect with evidence about its actual effect, including trade-offs and unintended consequences.
